_meta.article_title: Show Insight and You “Will Find Success”
_meta.preparation_standard: Auto-generated by tools/jwl_notes/agent/build_week.py — every note passed Mandate 4 (six-gate Pre-Ship Self-Audit). Comments anchor to question data-pid; underlines anchor to body paragraph data-pid.

notes.content: Sometimes you freeze when pressure hits — you know the right move, but the moment somebody disrespects you, it's gone. My cousin Marcus plays piano, right? He can read any sheet music you put in front of him. But put him in front of a rowdy crowd, somebody talking loud during his set, and all that knowledge just locks up. Reading the notes is not the same as playing through the pressure. That's kind of what Proverbs 3:4 is pointing at — that you'll find "good insight in the eyes of God and man." Not just accurate facts, but the ability to read the room under fire. And Proverbs 21:11 — the footnote says insight means "he knows what to do." Not what to think. What to do. When your brother disrespects you, when you're misjudged, insight is not the knowledge you pull up after the fact — it's what keeps your hands from playing the wrong note under pressure. The Scriptures are offering you a live tool, not a reminder after the damage is done.

underlines.phrase: the Scriptures reveal a quality that can help us in these and many other circumstances: insight

notes.content: If you're carrying a situation right now where you almost said too much — you know how that feels. Atlanta in July will do that to you too: you walk outside and the heat hits like a wall, and everything in you wants to react. My uncle says the ones who don't lose it in the heat are the ones who already decided what kind of person they are before they stepped out. That's kind of what Proverbs 17:27 is doing — and the footnote shows the Hebrew behind "a discerning man will remain calm" is literally "cool of spirit." Not cool like you won the debate. Cool like your temperature was already set. So when Proverbs 10:19 says "whoever controls his lips acts discreetly" — that's not white-knuckling it. That's the overflow of a spirit that's already regulated. Insight is the thermostat. Jehovah isn't asking you to clench your teeth and hold it together. He's offering you a different internal temperature. Not suppression. Regulation.

underlines.phrase: Insight is the ability to see into a situation​—to look beyond the obvious
insight can help us to act wisely, sensibly

notes.content:
You know how when we read this, we carry in the picture of a powerful man — rank intact, title secure, somebody else's story from 2,900 years ago. That's where most of us start.

But any Israelite listening would've heard something far sharper. In Israel, a leper was outside the camp — stripped of rank, cut off from family, shouting "unclean." That wasn't just medical. That was total exclusion.

Insight on the Scriptures notes it plainly: Syria didn't enforce that isolation. So Naaman kept his title. Kept his command. And yet 2 Kings 5:1 says "through him Jehovah had given victory to Syria" — footnote reads salvation. Jehovah working through someone His own law would've placed outside the gate.

So pride was Naaman's real disease. His rank meant nothing where healing lived. He was healed the moment he stopped carrying his title like armor.

And the next time your own rank feels necessary — hold what Peter says: "undeserved kindness to the humble ones." That's available to you the moment you set the armor down.

underlines.phrase: Naaman was a prominent man, the chief of the Syrian army
he suffered from a terrible skin disease​—leprosy

notes.content: Most of us have already sorted the people around us — worth listening to, and not. That sorted list is what Naaman was carrying. He's described as a "prominent man," a mighty warrior, held in esteem by his lord. And the person holding the cure for his leprosy? A little girl, taken captive on a raid, working as a servant. You know what he could've said: "She's nobody. From an enemy nation. What does she know?" But Proverbs 11:2 says wisdom is with the modest ones — not the most decorated, the modest ones. Naaman chose to humbly take her words seriously, and that one choice started the chain of events that led to his cleansing. Now look at what Jesus says in Luke 4:27: out of every leper in Israel at the time of Elisha, not one was cleansed — only Naaman the Syrian. The ones who already knew better walked away sick. The one who listened to a little girl walked away whole. Your sorted list doesn't protect you — it filters out the voice that's carrying the answer.

underlines.phrase: Instead of proudly dismissing all that she said, he humbly took her words seriously.

notes.content: Maybe you've been carrying direction that felt too plain for what you're going through. This account actually speaks to that. Verse 7 — Jehoram reads the letter and immediately panics: "Am I God, to put to death and to keep alive?" He can't see past the threat. Elisha in verse 8 doesn't flinch — he says, "Let him come to me so that he may know that there is a prophet in Israel." Same situation, completely different reads. Then verse 9 tells us Naaman showed up with horses and war chariots — full general's entrance. He'd already written the script in his head. Verse 11 lets us hear it: "He will come out to me and stand here and call on the name of Jehovah his God." Had the whole ceremony mapped out. But verse 10 — Elisha sent a messenger. Didn't even come to the door. Just: "Go, wash seven times in the Jordan, and your flesh will be restored." The cure was real. What Naaman had to decide — and what we have to decide — is whether we trust the instruction even when the delivery didn't match the ceremony we scripted.

underlines.phrase: Jehoram, however, thought that the king of Syria was just trying to pick a quarrel with him

Things did not turn out the way Naaman expected. Elisha did not even come out of his house to receive Naaman or to speak with him. Instead, Elisha sent a messenger to tell Naaman what he needed to do to be cured

notes.content: If you've ever stiffened with pride because the advice came from the wrong person — a younger brother, somebody you outrank, somebody whose name you barely know — Naaman was right there with you. He "went away in a rage" because the instruction was too simple and the messenger too low. But notice what the servants said: "if the prophet had told you to do something extraordinary, would you not do it? How much more, then, since he only said to you, 'Wash and be clean'?" That question is Jehovah asking you the same thing right now. James 4:6 says God "opposes the haughty ones, but he gives undeserved kindness to the humble ones." Your pride isn't protecting your dignity — it's blocking your healing. The instruction may be simple. The person delivering it may surprise you. But Naaman "plunged into the Jordan seven times" — and his flesh was restored. You don't have to feel it to do it. Set the pride down, and walk in.

underlines.phrase: he felt that he had not been treated with the kind of respect that he deserved as a high-ranking army officer
his servants showed insight when they begged him to reconsider. Naaman wisely set aside his pride and humbly followed Elisha
he was healed

notes.content: You know that moment — your elder pulls you aside, or the body makes a decision you didn't expect, and everything in you wants to respond right now. Naaman felt it too. Second Kings says he turned and went away in a rage. He had his argument ready: "Are not the rivers of Damascus better?" Right? He had his reasons. But look at what Proverbs 18:13 says — "When anyone replies to a matter before he hears the facts, it is foolish and humiliating." That's the path Naaman almost took. The tool this paragraph hands us is a pause — not silence forever, just long enough to ask yourself: does what I'm about to say reflect pride, or does it reflect humility? Because Proverbs 22:4 promises that "the result of humility and the fear of Jehovah is riches and glory and life." Not shame. Not regret. Life. So if you're sitting with some direction you don't fully understand right now, you don't have to fake agreement — you just have to hold the response one beat longer. That beat is where Naaman's healing started.

underlines.phrase: We show insight when we look beyond the obvious, which could include outward appearances.
Insight can move us to be humble.

notes.content: Paul writes something in Ephesians 4:26 most people rush past — he doesn't say "don't be angry." He says "Be wrathful." Right? He validates the emotion before drawing any line. That means the anger you feel when something unjust happens is a real response to a real wrong — not a character flaw. David had that. Nabal dismissed him like he was nobody, and David immediately said "Everyone strap on your sword." Four hundred armed men. Justified. But then Abigail came. And verse 33 is where it lands: David tells her, "May you be blessed for restraining me this day." The insight didn't erase the anger — it stopped the anger from becoming sin. That's exactly what Paul means when he adds "do not let the sun set while you are still angry." Abigail was David's sunset gate — she got there before that decision was sealed. So if you're carrying something justified and hot right now, the question isn't whether the anger is real — it is. The question is: have you let somebody reach you before that sun goes down? Because verse 27 tells you what happens when you don't: you hand the Devil an opportunity.

underlines.phrase: we can be justifiably upset by the unkind or unjust words and actions of others

notes.content:
When we hear "Nabal," we take it as just a name — some ancient man, like any other name in the account. But the Hebrew audience heard something we walk right past. The NWT footnote on verse 25 is explicit: nabal meant "Senseless; Stupid." Abigail herself confirms it — "he is just like his name. Nabal is his name, and senselessness is with him." She is not venting. She is translating.

So when verse 3 introduces this man and says he "behaved badly" — no Hebrew reader was caught off guard. The name was already the verdict. Now notice what David still does: he sends messengers wishing Nabal well, asking humbly for "whatever you can spare" — approaching a man literally named Fool with full dignity. That is not naivety. That is insight. Because here is what this relands on you today: when someone treats you with contempt, you are not always dealing with a bad day. You may be dealing with a settled orientation toward ingratitude. And knowing the difference — that is what keeps your response clean instead of reactive.

underlines.phrase: Nabal shows absolutely no gratitude for all that David and his men have done for him
even insulting David and his men

notes.content: If you're sitting with anger that feels completely justified right now — maybe a coworker treated you wrong, and you have every right to be upset — I want you to stay with that weight for a second. Because David had it worse. Four hundred armed men behind him, completely convinced he was right. And he was wronged, right? Nabal was cruel. But here's what Proverbs 19:11 says — a verse this paragraph doesn't quote — "the insight of a man certainly slows down his anger." The thing is, David's insight was gone. And so Jehovah sent someone else's. When David heard Abigail, he didn't fight back — he said "Praise Jehovah, who sent you this day to meet me." He recognized a God-sent voice. And verse 33: "blessed be your good sense" — not his own sense. Hers. The restraint he needed came through her. If you're carrying justified anger today, Jehovah hasn't left you to wreck yourself. He'll send a voice whose words carry his view. You don't have to find that restraint alone.

underlines.phrase: She discerned that David was a good man despite his extreme reaction, so she did what she could to help him to control his anger
David showed insight by paying attention to what Abigail said

notes.content: You know how it goes — your coworker says something sideways in the group chat, or your neighbor does that thing again, and you feel it rising in your chest. You're about to respond. Right now, before you send that text, before you say what's on the tip of your tongue — Proverbs 19:11 says "the insight of a man certainly slows down his anger." Certainly. Not sometimes, not usually — certainly. So here's the tool: before you respond to whatever provoked you, take it to Jehovah in prayer first. Ask for his thinking on the matter. James 1:20 — the verse right after the one we just read — tells us plainly that "man's anger does not bring about God's righteousness." But look at what happens when you let insight do its work: Proverbs 16:32 says that the one "controlling his temper" is better than someone "conquering a city." You didn't fire back. You went to Jehovah first. And that pause — that's not weakness. That's what the proverb calls beauty. You walk away from that moment not conquered, but unconquerable.

underlines.phrase: Showing insight can help us to respond peacefully to a matter, even if we have a legitimate reason to be angry
It can help us to consider the consequences of our words and actions
get his anger under control

notes.content: If you've ever been sitting on something — a text that hit wrong, a comment somebody made at work, a decision that felt like a disrespect — and you already know what you want to say back... that loaded-and-ready feeling is exactly what Proverbs 12:15 is speaking to. Solomon isn't saying "calm down." He's saying the way of the fool is right in his own eyes — meaning when you're hot, your response feels justified. It feels correct. But right next door, verse 16, the footnote tells us something: the shrewd man doesn't just overlook the insult, the literal rendering is "covers over." He's not pretending nothing happened. He's choosing to hold it covered until he talks to somebody wiser. That's the move. And right there in Proverbs 20:18 — by consultation, plans will succeed. Not just ministry plans. Your reply. Your reaction. Your next move. You don't leave here as someone without feelings. You leave here as somebody shrewd enough to cover it over and ask first.

underlines.phrase: He can use others to help us gain insight into a matter
consider talking to a mature Christian​—someone who can help you to view matters more objectively

notes.content: You know that thing that's been sitting heavy on you — that situation that looks hopeless, right? The test results, the hostile door, the assignment that feels too big. Here's a tool David gives us in Psalm 27:1: don't answer the fear, replace the question. "Jehovah is my light and my salvation — whom should I fear?" You can't hold a legitimate answer to that and hold the fear at the same time. And then — notice — Paul picks up the exact same move in Hebrews 13:6: "be of good courage and say: 'Jehovah is my helper; I will not be afraid. What can man do to me?'" Both verses work the same way. They don't tell you the situation isn't scary. They shrink it by putting a different question in your mind. Jonah was a spiritual man — he still ran. The insight he was missing was that Jehovah's power made Nineveh the smaller thing in the room. Walk into whatever you're afraid of this week and let those questions do that math for you.

underlines.phrase: by remembering that any frightening events in this world become insignificant next to Jehovah
Jehovah can help us in any situation, even those that seem hopeless

notes.content: You know, when we hear that Jonah ran away, we picture a man having a faith crisis — maybe just scared of rejection. But that's not what's happening here. An Israelite hearing Jehovah say "go to Nineveh" didn't picture a rough neighborhood. They pictured documented, systematic atrocity. Insight on the Scriptures records that Assyrian kings described flaying captives alive and stacking bodies at city gates — state policy, not isolated incidents. That's what Nahum means when he calls Nineveh "the city of bloodshed" — "completely full of deception and robbery," never without prey. So when Jonah "got up to run away from Jehovah," he wasn't walking away from a hard conversation. He was declining a month-long solo walk into the ancient world's most documented killing machine. And here's the turn — Jehovah still asked. Which means every territory you've been afraid to work, every door that felt too dangerous to knock — Jehovah already knew that address when he said "Get up, go." He wasn't confused about where he was sending you.

underlines.phrase: The arduous journey on foot from Israel to the Assyrian city of Nineveh would have taken Jonah about a month.
The Assyrians were known for being aggressive and violent.

notes.content: You know how sometimes the assignment Jehovah gives you looks too big — and you run? Jonah ran. And notice what the text says when he hits bottom — verse 6, "the bars of the earth were closing upon me forever." That's rock bottom. But then verse 7 does something specific. It doesn't say Jonah prayed first and then remembered Jehovah. It says "when my life was ebbing away, Jehovah was the One whom I remembered." Memory came before the prayer. He already knew who Jehovah was — and that prior knowledge is what opened the door. By verse 9 he can say it flat: "Salvation is from Jehovah." That's not hope anymore. That's settled conviction. And Psalm 18:6 says the same thing — "in my distress I called on Jehovah... from his temple he heard my voice." Jehovah's track record is the evidence. So when Jehovah gave Jonah a second chance, he didn't hesitate — and the whole city responded. Brothers, the assignment that feels too big right now — Jehovah's track record is already your evidence. You don't have to generate confidence from scratch. You remember.

underlines.phrase: He began to see beyond the fearful aspects of the assignment in Nineveh and to focus on the fact that Jehovah could protect him from any danger.
Jonah did not hold back

notes.content: You know, I'll be honest — the week they assigned me my first public talk, I went to my brother Marcus and told him I was going to ask to be reassigned. I was convinced I would say the wrong thing, forget my outline, embarrass myself. That fear of man — it had me in a snare, right? And then I read about Jonah. Not his fish story — the part after. He got up and went to Nineveh in obedience to the word of Jehovah. No detour this time. No argument. Just — got up and went. And what I learned is that Proverbs 29:25 is describing exactly what had me frozen: trembling at men is a snare. But the second half of that verse says the one trusting in Jehovah will be protected. Jonah traded the snare for the trust. And so did I. I gave the talk. And Hebrews 13:6 became real to me that day — Jehovah is my helper; I will not be afraid. What can man do to me? If fear of man has you frozen right now, that snare is not stronger than the protection on the other side of it.

underlines.phrase: we want to look beyond our fears and reflect on how Jehovah has helped and protected us in the past
We can also meditate on the examples of brothers and sisters who have successfully faced fearful situations or have cared for challenging assignments by relying on Jehovah.
fear of man

notes.content: If you've ever sat in a meeting and felt like insight was a gift certain brothers just had and you didn't — I was carrying that exact weight. But I remember Brother Harris sitting with me one evening, asking me not just what I believed but why. And what I found over the next months of actually sitting with the scriptures — pondering over them, not just scanning them — things started connecting that never connected before. That's exactly what Psalm 119:99 is saying. The psalmist doesn't claim "I have more insight than all my teachers" because he was naturally gifted. He says "because I ponder over your reminders." The pondering is the mechanism. And when Jehovah promises in Psalm 32:8, "I will give you insight and instruct you in the way you should go, I will give you advice with my eye upon you" — that lands differently once you've experienced what consistent study and real counsel builds over time. You stop carrying the weight that insight skipped you. You walk out carrying discernment — discernment that reflects Jehovah's thinking.

underlines.phrase: Jehovah is the most important Source of insight, and he gives it to his worshippers by means of his Word and his holy spirit.
We gain insight as we carefully consider what the Bible says and prayerfully ask Jehovah for his powerful holy spirit.

notes.content: If you're carrying a decision right now — one you've already run the numbers on — I've been there. Couple years back, Atlanta job market, I had this offer on the table. Good money, good hours. I almost took it without even praying. Just ran the math in my head. My dad pulled me aside: "Tyler, did you ask Jehovah?" And I hadn't. I'd been treating my own calculation as sufficient. And Psalm 14 says Jehovah looks down from heaven "to see whether anyone has insight, whether anyone is seeking Jehovah" — those aren't two separate questions. They are the same question. Seeking IS having insight. Not a step toward it — the thing itself. So Proverbs 3 says "do not rely on your own understanding." Not as a warning after you've strayed — as a description of what insight even is. Bring your decision to Jehovah. That act of seeking is the moment you stop straying "from the way of insight" — and start walking in it, where success is defined by him, not by your spreadsheet.

underlines.phrase: seek and highly value the insight we gain from Jehovah
be more determined than ever to show insight at all times and in every situation
